newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - 28th April.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - 28th April.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
- KVAERNER AND BOEING IN FIVE BILLION DOLLAR BASE DEAL

Boeing of the US has teamed up with Anglo-Norwegian engineering and construction group Kvaerner in a 5 billion dollar project to develop the first ever off-shore air base for the US Navy. The base will be 1,600 metres long and be able to handle a variety of aircraft, housing up to 10,000 troops. The platforms will be built in Scandinavia and North America.
-- FIRST ELECTRONIC TAX RETURN FILED TO REVENUE

A Somerset firm of chartered accountants has filed the first electronic return to the Inland Revenue using the IR's Electronic Lodgement System which guarantees a direct and secure link between taxpayer agents and the central computer systems. The link is a part of the new self-assessment tax system for 8.5 million taxpayers not part of the PAYE system.
-- OFGAS WARNS OF POSSIBLE CONFLICT ON PRICE CONTROL

UK gas industry regulator Ofgas, has warned the Monopolies and Mergers Commission that if its report into pipeline price controls is not tough enough, it could be in constant conflict with BG. Ofgas is considering pursuing a policy of unbundling ancillary services, which could leave BG with stranded assets it has invested in, but which may no longer be viable in a competitive market.
-- KOHL STANDS FIRM ON EMU TIMETABLE

German chancellor Helmut Kohl is standing firm on his demands that the Emu launch date not be delayed any longer than the current 1999 deadline. Kohl made it clear Germany is determined to meet the timetable and downplayed statements by his senior advisers that a delay of up to two years would be preferable to a single currency based on anything less.
-- UTILITIES MAY FACE DATA PROBE

The UK data protection watchdog has advised the registrar to begin proceedings against three more utilities, all regional electricity companies, for using customer databases to sell other services. British Gas Transco, and Southern Electric had previously been warned of such offenses. The issue holds much importance, as the energy market will be freed next April.
-- IT SECTOR HIT BY PRESSURE ON SKILLS AND PAY

The UK association for IT software, CSSA, has declared that computer services and software companies in the UK face serious skills shortages and increasing wage costs which could stunt the sector's ambitious growth plans. The CSSA went on to add that the oncoming millennium bug and Emu issues would lead to worsening of the problems. The sector currently faces over 3,500 vacancies and the number is expected to increase to 14,500 over the next three years.
-- IBM EXCHANGES CHEAP DATA MINING FOR REVENUE SHARE

IBM has declared a "data warehousing" scheme in an attempt to prove the value of high-tech marketing programmes, offering to drop its prices in exchange for a cut of clients' profits. IBM doubt that in the long run clients will outsource the management of its customer databases. Data warehouses are electronic filing systems which can contain over 300 million pages of text.
-- PREMIER OIL DIRECTOR FACES OPPOSITION

The founder of Premier Oil, Roland Shaw, is set to vote against the re-election of one of his colleagues, Sam Laidlaw, due to what the calls a conflict of interest. Shaw believes that Laidlaw's involvement as chairman of US oil group Amerada Hess would cause problems with his position as non-executive director of Premier.
-- PEUGEOT UK JUMPS TO 30 MILLION STG BUT MARGINS TIGHT

The UK subsidiary of Peugot has seen a profit rise to 30.5 million in 1996, accounting for nearly half the French motoring group's earnings. Peugeot UK's managing director warned that due to intensifying UK market conditions, further pressure would be placed on margins as new car prices could not rise to match inflation.
-- ITG POISED TO BE FIRST TO JOIN IRISH JUNIOR MARKET

Irish communications service provider Independent Telecoms Group will be the first group to become a part of the Developing Companies Market, which is the Irish equivalent of London's Alternative Investment Market. The DCM hopes to attract up to 12 companies with a capitalisation range of IR3 million pounds and IR20 million pounds in an effort to counter the dearth of new issues on the main market
